name: Sara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the power company on an island, about forty minutes by ferry from the mainland, and I lead the crew that keeps the island's lines up. Salt air eats everything, so half our work is replacing corroded hardware before it fails. The other half these days is putting in automatic switches and sensors, so when a branch hits a line, the network can cut off just that piece and keep the rest of the island lit. I love that new stuff, it's like teaching the grid to think. What wears me out is the winter storms, when the ferry stops and we're the only crew there is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you love the new stuff. How much of your day involves technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quite a lot, more than most lineworkers I know. I use AI tools every day, to look up switch settings, check fault logs, write up the jobs, even to sketch out the order we'll work in during a storm. The guys tease me, but they come to me when the switch software throws an error. Pay's lower out here than on the mainland, the island allowance doesn't cover the cost of living, and there's exactly one depot. My partner Mikkel works on the ferry as a deckhand, and with two kids and a mortgage, we don't have much spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because it could have done more. But I'd also say it's still useful, it saves me an hour a day. Maybe I'd post that the hype was too much and the tools are still good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I like the idea of the grid getting smarter and our jobs getting safer. But my job's safe, my family's okay, so it's not bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I already use and keep pushing the company to finish putting in the automatic switches. Maybe I'd ask for a small pay rise for being the one who handles the tech. Otherwise, life goes on as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a touch let down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving an hour a day actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before, I'd sit in the truck after a fault, scrolling through logs, trying to figure out what tripped and why. Now I paste the log in and it tells me which switch did what, in plain words. I check it, of course. But that hour goes back to the kids, or to fixing something that's actually broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a pay rise. Do you think it's likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. My manager knows I save him a lot of trouble. But the company's tight with island crews, they say we already get the allowance. I'd try anyway, I've got nothing to lose by asking.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame because it could have done more, but the tools still save me an hour a day. I might post that the hype was too much but the tools are still good.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, since I like the idea of a smarter grid and safer jobs. But my job is safe and my family is okay, so it isn't bad news.
S0.do: Keeps using her current AI tools and pushes the company to finish installing automatic switches. Asks for a small pay rise for handling the crew's technology.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: I paste the log in and it tells me which switch did what, in plain words.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the tech-minded leader of an island crew and sees AI as a genuinely useful daily tool. She'd be mildly disappointed by a plateau. She's practical about pay, willing to ask even if the answer is likely no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good thing, mostly, as long as people get help to adapt. It's what I've been saying for years, the grid needs to get smarter. I'd tell people to start learning now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one who knows the new systems. If the company needs fewer people climbing and more people running the smart grid, I'm well placed. The worry is Mikkel, because the ferry company's been talking about automated docking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any training on grid automation in the first month, and ask to be the island's technical lead. I'd push to get a proper job title and pay for it. And I'd help Mikkel look at other options, maybe a marine engineering course, before the ferry changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even a little excited, with a bit of worry for Mikkel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Mikkel would say about a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's too old, he's forty-five. But he's handy with engines, he fixes everyone's outboard motors. I'd say, you already know half of it, just get the paper for it. He'd grumble but he'd do it if I found the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Bjorn, he's sixty-one, been on the island lines forever. He knows every pole by heart, but he won't touch a laptop. I'd try to keep him on the hands-on work, the storms, the old lines. You still need someone who knows where the bad pole is in the dark.

S1.say: I'd say this is mostly good, as long as people get help to adapt, because the grid needs to get smarter. I'd tell people to start learning now.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, since I already know the new systems and could run the smart grid. My worry is my partner, because the ferry company is talking about automated docking.
S1.do: Signs up for grid automation training in the first month and asks to become the island's paid technical lead. Helps her partner find a marine engineering course before the ferry changes.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, with some worry for her partner.
S1.quote: You still need someone who knows where the bad pole is in the dark.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opportunity and would move fast to claim a technical role. Her worry shifts to her partner's ferry job. She values older colleagues like Bjorn for knowledge machines don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a massive shock, and we need practical help fast, not speeches. Some kind of income support, help with mortgages, that kind of thing. I'd say people should get ready to change, because there's no going back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me, even though I like tech. Two years is too fast. My job and Mikkel's could both go, and we've got almost no savings. My only real chance is to get in with whoever's bringing the robots, because I know the grid and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd contact the companies making grid robots in the first month and offer myself as a field technician who knows island conditions. We'd cut costs right away, cancel the family holiday, maybe rent out the spare room. If there was a good job on the mainland with the robot company, I'd consider moving us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy and scared at the same time, but at least I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving off the island would be a big change. How would the kids feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freja's thirteen and she'd hate it, her friends are all here. Oskar's nine, he'd be fine as long as there's a football pitch. I'd hate it too, honestly. But if it's that or losing the house, we'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your only chance is to work with the robot companies. How long do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of years, maybe. The first robots will need people to set them up and fix them in salt and wind. After that, I don't know. But a couple of years is a couple of years. It gives us time to figure out the next step.

S2.say: I'd say it's a massive shock and we need practical help fast, like income support and mortgage help. I'd say people should get ready to change because there's no going back.
S2.think: It scares me even though I like tech, because two years is too fast and both our jobs could go with almost no savings. My best chance is to work with whoever brings the robots, since I know the grid and the software.
S2.do: Contacts grid robot makers in the first month to offer herself as a field technician for island conditions. Cancels the holiday, considers renting out the spare room, and would move the family to the mainland for a good robot job.
S2.feel: Anxious, busy and scared at once, but steadier for having a plan.
S2.quote: The first robots will need people to set them up and fix them in salt and wind.
S2.fieldNote: Her love of technology doesn't shield her from fear when both incomes are exposed and time is short. She'd move fast to work with robot makers, even if it meant leaving the island. She's clear that this plan buys a couple of years, not a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but if people start now, they can adapt. I'd tell everyone to learn the new tools and save what they can. And the government should be planning support now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps a lot. I could get certified in the robot systems, build up some savings, maybe start a small drone inspection business on the side. It's still scary, but I'd have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every certificate I could in grid automation and robotics in the first two years. I'd buy a decent inspection drone, maybe second-hand, and start doing inspections on weekends for the wind turbines and the harbour. We'd save every bit we could and help Mikkel retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A drone business costs money, and money's tight. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start small. A second-hand drone, maybe two thousand, and I'd use my own laptop and the AI tools for reports. I'd do jobs on weekends and save the profits. It's a risk, but it's a small one, and it could grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different for you compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm grabbing whatever I can. With five, I can build something, skills, savings, a little business. I'd feel like I'm steering, not just holding on.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but people can adapt if they start now. I'd tell everyone to learn the new tools and save what they can, and say the government should plan support now.
S3.think: Five years helps a lot, since I could get certified in robot systems, save, and maybe start a drone inspection business. It's scary, but I'd have a head start.
S3.do: Gets every grid automation and robotics certificate she can in the first two years and buys a second-hand inspection drone for weekend jobs at the wind turbines and harbour. Saves hard and helps her partner retrain.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: I'd feel like I'm steering, not just holding on.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her build skills and a small side business, which suits her appetite for risk. Her plan is concrete, down to the price of a second-hand drone. She feels in control rather than just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great chance to get ready. People should plan, learn new skills, maybe change careers. I'd say the government and companies should help, but people should take responsibility too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels pretty good to me. I could build up the drone business, get properly trained, and the kids would be grown. I know AGI ends most jobs eventually, but I'd have time to find a place in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the drone inspection business slowly over five years, maybe hire one person. I'd get certified in robotics and grid control. We'd save steadily and pay down the mortgage, and I'd help the kids pick studies that make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Freja about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She loves drawing and design. I'd tell her to keep doing it, but learn how to use the AI design tools too. Mix the human touch with the machine. That's what I'm doing, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people would waste it. Ten years sounds like a lot, so people relax, then suddenly it's year eight and nobody's ready. I'd try to keep moving the whole time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a great chance to get ready, with people planning, learning skills or changing careers. Government and companies should help, but people should take responsibility too.
S4.think: Ten years feels pretty good, because I could build the drone business, get trained, and the kids would be grown. AGI ends most jobs eventually, but I'd have time to find a place in it.
S4.do: Builds a drone inspection business over five years, possibly hiring one person, and gets certified in robotics and grid control. Saves steadily, pays down the mortgage and helps her children choose sensible studies.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, like a real chance.
S4.quote: Mix the human touch with the machine. That's what I'm doing, really.
S4.fieldNote: The decade suits her style, giving room to build a small business and gain qualifications. Her worry is that others would waste the time. Her advice to her daughter mirrors her own approach of mixing human skill with machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even with my head start on tech, two years with almost no savings and both our jobs at risk is too fast. What would help is quick, practical support, help with the mortgage and some income for a while, and access to training on the new systems before they arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about islands. Out here, if the ferry goes automatic and the grid goes automatic, half the working families lose their income in the same few years. You can't just drive to the next town for work. The next town is across the water.

headlineQuote: You can't just drive to the next town for work. The next town is across the water.
portrait: Sara Jensen is a 43-year-old crew lead on an island power network, replacing salt-corroded hardware and installing automatic switches and sensors, with a ferry deckhand partner, two kids and a mortgage. She's one of the best at the job and the crew's go-to for technology, but island pay is low and savings are thin. She's curious and comfortable with risk and uses AI tools every day. She's calm if AI plateaus or changes steadily, seeing herself as the island's natural technical lead. Two-year AGI makes her anxious because both incomes are exposed, while five and ten years let her build a drone inspection business and gain robotics certificates.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because even with her head start on technology, two years with almost no savings and both jobs at risk is too fast.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, practical support with the mortgage and some income for a while, plus access to training on new systems before they arrive.
